briefing.text: Nine days ago, a Castellan strategist named Nadia Marr walked into a federal building in Ottawa with a hard drive and a warning.
Castellan Group runs a third of this country's groceries, half its pharmacies, and the data behind both. Their CEO, Adrian Voss, calls the next phase Meridian.
Meridian buys up the suppliers a town depends on, then uses everything Castellan knows about each household to decide who gets supplied, and at what price.
Marketing is supposed to be a trade. You create value for customers and you capture value in return. Meridian keeps the second half and throws away the first.
Joint Task Force LEDGER exists to prove it before launch. Tonight, Castellan's regional directors meet at Fulfillment Centre 7 in Hamilton.
Your target is Paul Ostrowski, the director who built Meridian's customer model. We take him alive, and we take their customer doctrine files with him.
Sergeant Wren, Corporal Ruiz: you're on the ground. Dr. Marr is on comms. Castellan Security Services will be armed and they will not hesitate.

debrief.text: Ostrowski talked for six hours. Meridian's money comes from inside Castellan: one division is quietly funding the whole thing.
Then we cut the money. Get some rest. Next stop is Ottawa.

r.text: Wren, Ruiz, you're through the fence. Castellan Security patrols the yard in pairs.
Rain's loud. Good. Means they won't hear us coming.
Every CSS guard you see is protecting a warehouse full of other people's groceries. Keep that in mind tonight.

post.text: Yard's clear.
There's a laptop in the guard post. Castellan onboards every employee with the same deck. Grab it.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]WHAT IS MARKETING?[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing[/b] is the process by which companies engage customers, build strong customer relationships, and create customer value in order to capture value from customers in return.

It is not just selling and advertising. Selling is only the tip of the iceberg. The goal is to satisfy customer needs.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE MARKETING PROCESS: FIVE STEPS[/color][/font_size]

  •  1. Understand the marketplace and customer needs and wants.

  •  2. Design a customer value-driven marketing strategy.

  •  3. Construct an integrated marketing program that delivers superior value.

  •  4. Engage customers, build profitable relationships, and create customer delight.

  •  5. Capture value from customers to create profits and customer equity.

The first four steps create value FOR customers. The last step captures value FROM customers in return.

calls.q: The Castellan deck says the first four steps of the marketing process do one thing and the fifth does another. What does the fifth step do?
a: Captures value from customers in return
calls.why: Steps 1 to 4 create value for customers. Step 5 captures value from them: sales, profits and customer equity. Meridian skips straight to step five.

calls.q: How does the textbook define marketing?
a: Engaging customers, building strong relationships and creating customer value in order to capture value in return
Selling and advertising products to as many people as possible
Producing goods efficiently and distributing them widely
Persuading customers to buy products they would not otherwise buy
calls.why: Selling and advertising are only part of marketing. The definition centres on creating customer value and relationships, then capturing value back.

wall: Wants: needs shaped by culture + personality
Demands: wants backed by buying power

r.text: Trucks are lined up. Castellan branding on every trailer.
Read the trailers. That's the whole business in one sentence: they sell people answers to needs.
Contacts on the docks. Clear them.

post.text: Ostrowski's team left a field memo on the dispatch desk. It explains how they see the people on the other end of those trucks.

intel.t: Field Memo: Needs Are Not Optional
intel.src: P. Ostrowski · internal memo · Meridian working group
intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]NEEDS, WANTS AND DEMANDS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Needs[/b] are states of felt deprivation. They include basic physical needs for food, clothing, warmth and safety; social needs for belonging and affection; and individual needs for knowledge and self-expression. Marketers did not create these needs. They are a basic part of the human makeup.

[b]Wants[/b] are the form human needs take as they are shaped by culture and individual personality. A hungry person in Hamilton wants a sandwich and a coffee; a hungry person somewhere else wants something else.

[b]Demands[/b] are human wants that are backed by buying power. Given their wants and resources, people demand the products with the benefits that add up to the most value and satisfaction.

Note from P.O.: A need cannot be declined. A town that needs insulin will find buying power somewhere. Meridian prices to that fact.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKET OFFERINGS[/color][/font_size]

Consumers' needs and wants are fulfilled through [b]market offerings[/b]: some combination of products, services, information, or experiences offered to a market to satisfy a need or want.

Offerings are not limited to physical products. They also include services, events, persons, places, organizations, information and ideas.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING MYOPIA[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing myopia[/b] is the mistake of paying more attention to the specific products a company offers than to the benefits and experiences produced by these products.

A drill manufacturer may think the customer needs a drill. What the customer really needs is a hole. Myopic sellers are left in trouble when a new product serves the customer's need better or less expensively.

calls.q: Ostrowski writes that a town 'needs' insulin and will 'find buying power somewhere.' In textbook terms, a want backed by buying power is a...
calls.why: Needs are states of felt deprivation; wants are needs shaped by culture and personality; demands are wants backed by buying power.

calls.q: A Castellan pharmacy manager says: 'We sell blood-glucose meters.' The customer actually buys control over their health. Ignoring that difference is...
calls.why: Marketing myopia is focusing on the specific product instead of the benefits and experiences it produces. The drill, not the hole.

calls.q: Which of these is NOT a market offering in the textbook's sense?
calls.why: Market offerings are combinations of products, services, information or experiences. Felt deprivation is a need, not an offering.

wall: Perceived value = all benefits − all costs

r.text: Sorting hall. Heavy CSS presence. Expect them to fall back to the conveyors.
Copy. Wren, take left, I've got right.
Look at the volume on those belts. Castellan understood value once. That's why customers came.

post.text: Hall clear. Moving up.
Their customer value report is on the supervisor's terminal. That's the one I'd want if I were trying to understand why people stay.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CUSTOMER VALUE AND SATISFACTION[/color][/font_size]

Customers form expectations about the value and satisfaction that various market offerings will deliver and buy accordingly.

Satisfied customers buy again and tell others about their good experiences. Dissatisfied customers often switch to competitors and disparage the product to others.

Marketers must set the right level of expectations. Set them too low and they may satisfy those who buy but fail to attract enough buyers. Set them too high and buyers will be disappointed.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]EXCHANGES AND RELATIONSHIPS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Exchange[/b] is the act of obtaining a desired object from someone by offering something in return.

Marketing consists of actions taken to build and maintain desirable exchange relationships with target audiences involving a product, service, idea or other object. Beyond simply attracting new customers and creating transactions, the goal is to retain customers and grow their business.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETS[/color][/font_size]

A [b]market[/b] is the set of all actual and potential buyers of a product or service. These buyers share a particular need or want that can be satisfied through exchange relationships.

Marketing means managing markets to bring about profitable customer relationships. Sellers search for buyers, identify their needs, design good market offerings, set prices for them, promote them, and store and deliver them.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE MODERN MARKETING SYSTEM[/color][/font_size]

A company and its competitors research the market and interact with consumers to understand their needs. Then they create and exchange market offerings, messages and other marketing content with consumers, either directly or through marketing intermediaries.

Each party in the system adds value for the next level. All of the arrows represent relationships that must be developed and managed. Major environmental forces (demographic, economic, natural, technological, political and cultural) shape the whole system.

calls.q: A family compares Castellan's delivery service with a rival's: faster, but twice the price. Their evaluation of all the benefits minus all the costs, relative to the competitor, is called...
calls.why: Customer-perceived value is the customer's evaluation of the difference between all the benefits and all the costs of an offer, relative to competing offers.

calls.q: Customer satisfaction depends on...
a: How a product's perceived performance matches the buyer's expectations
How much the company spends on advertising
The number of competitors in the market
The lifetime value of the customer
calls.why: Satisfaction is the extent to which perceived performance matches expectations. Below expectations: dissatisfied. Matching or exceeding: satisfied or delighted.

calls.q: The textbook defines a market as...
a: The set of all actual and potential buyers of a product or service
The place where products are physically sold
All the companies competing in an industry
The customers who bought from you last year
calls.why: A market is all actual and potential buyers who share a need or want that can be satisfied through exchange.

r.text: CSS training floor. Pop-up targets, scoreboard, the works.
Their target system is still networked. I can load my own labels onto it. Call it a refresher.
Make it quick. Ostrowski's meeting started twenty minutes ago.

drills.call: Five steps of the marketing process. Shoot them in order.
Now the five core marketplace concepts. Any order. Leave the decoys standing.

wall: Selling: push hard or they won't buy

r.text: Five directors in the glass room above you. One of them is Ostrowski. Castellan scrubbed their faces from every system, so we go by how they think.
I'm feeding you their intercepted audio. Ostrowski believes customers won't buy enough unless you push them hard. That's the selling concept.
Scope each director, listen, and mark the one who thinks like a salesman. Mark the wrong man and this whole room goes loud early.

post.text: Got him! Ostrowski's secured. Zip-tied and breathing.
You think this stops Meridian? Voss will have a new model by Monday.
The others were never the problem. Grab the orientation brief from the boardroom table.

intel.t: Five Ways to Run a Company
intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING MANAGEMENT[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing management[/b] is the art and science of choosing target markets and building profitable relationships with them. There are five alternative concepts under which organizations design and carry out marketing strategies.

[b]Production concept[/b]: consumers will favour products that are available and highly affordable, so the organization should focus on improving production and distribution efficiency. Risk: focusing too narrowly on operations and losing sight of satisfying customer needs.

[b]Product concept[/b]: consumers will favour products that offer the most quality, performance and innovative features, so the organization should devote its energy to continuous product improvement. Risk: marketing myopia.

[b]Selling concept[/b]: consumers will not buy enough of the firm's products unless it undertakes a large-scale selling and promotion effort. Typically practised with unsought goods. It focuses on creating sales transactions rather than long-term relationships.

[b]Marketing concept[/b]: achieving organizational goals depends on knowing the needs and wants of target markets and delivering the desired satisfactions better than competitors do. Selling takes an inside-out perspective; the marketing concept takes an outside-in perspective.

[b]Societal marketing concept[/b]: marketing decisions should consider consumers' wants, the company's requirements, consumers' long-run interests and society's long-run interests. Sustainable marketing calls for socially and environmentally responsible actions that meet present needs while preserving the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

calls.q: The selling concept starts with the factory and focuses on existing products. The marketing concept starts with...
a: A well-defined market and customer needs
calls.why: Selling is inside-out: factory, products, selling, profit through volume. Marketing is outside-in: market, customer needs, integrated marketing, profit through customer relationships.

calls.q: Director Achebe says 'the best product wins.' What's the textbook's warning about that philosophy?
a: It can lead to marketing myopia
It only works for unsought goods
It is the same as the societal marketing concept
calls.why: The product concept focuses on continuous product improvement and can lead to marketing myopia: loving the product, forgetting the need.

calls.q: Which orientation adds consumers' long-run interests and society's long-run interests to the marketing concept?
calls.why: The societal marketing concept balances consumer wants, company requirements, consumers' long-run interests and society's long-run interests.

directors.name: Director Halvorsen
directors.quote: Make it available everywhere and make it cheap. If we keep production efficient, customers will come to us.

directors.name: Director Achebe
directors.quote: The best product wins. Highest quality, most features, constant improvement. That's all the strategy we need.

directors.name: Director Ostrowski
directors.quote: People don't buy enough unless you make them. Big campaigns, aggressive selling. Push it, close it, move on.

directors.name: Director Lindqvist
directors.quote: Find out what customers need and want, then deliver it better than anyone else. Customer focus, not product focus.

directors.name: Director Mbeki
directors.quote: Customers' wants, our profits, and their long-run well-being. And society's. If we ignore that, it catches up with us.

r.text: CSS knows we're here. They'll try to purge the records office. Don't let them.
Moving Ostrowski behind cover. Wren, push.
The relationship files are in there. How Castellan builds loyalty, and how they decide who deserves it.

post.text: They didn't wipe the CRM handbook. Read it. It's the reason people trusted Castellan in the first place.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CUSTOMER RELATIONSHIP MANAGEMENT[/color][/font_size]

[b]Customer relationship management (CRM)[/b] is the overall process of building and maintaining profitable customer relationships by delivering superior customer value and satisfaction. It deals with all aspects of acquiring, engaging and growing customers.

The key to building lasting customer relationships is to create superior customer value and satisfaction.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]RELATIONSHIP LEVELS AND TOOLS[/color][/font_size]

Companies can build customer relationships at many levels. With many low-margin customers, a company may seek basic relationships. With a few high-margin customers, it may want full partnerships.

Beyond consistently high value and satisfaction, marketers use tools such as frequency marketing programs that reward customers who buy frequently or in large amounts, and club programs that offer members special benefits.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CUSTOMER-PERCEIVED VALUE[/color][/font_size]

[b]Customer-perceived value[/b] is the customer's evaluation of the difference between all the benefits and all the costs of a market offering relative to those of competing offers. Customers often do not judge values and costs accurately or objectively. They act on perceived value.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CUSTOMER ENGAGEMENT IN A DIGITAL, MOBILE, SOCIAL AGE[/color][/font_size]

Today's marketers are using new tools for connecting with customers, and customers have more information and more power than ever.

[b]Customer-engagement marketing[/b] means making the brand a meaningful part of consumers' conversations and lives by fostering direct and continuous customer involvement in shaping brand conversations, experiences and community. The aim is brand advocacy: satisfied customers who tell others about the brand.

[b]Customer-managed relationships[/b]: in the digital era, customers increasingly control the relationship. Marketers must practise marketing by attraction, creating offerings and content that engage customers rather than interrupt them.

[b]Consumer-generated marketing[/b] is brand exchanges created by consumers themselves, both invited and uninvited, by which consumers play an increasing role in shaping their own brand experiences and those of other consumers: reviews, videos, posts.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PARTNERS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Partner relationship management[/b] means working closely with partners in other company departments and outside the company to jointly bring greater value to customers. Inside, every department can be customer-facing. Outside, supply chain partners and alliances matter.

calls.q: Castellan customers post unboxing videos and reviews on their own, some praising, some furious. These are examples of...
calls.why: Consumer-generated marketing is brand exchanges created by consumers themselves, invited or uninvited.

calls.q: Castellan's pharmacy and grocery divisions share data so a customer only fills out one form. Working with other departments and outside firms to jointly deliver more customer value is...
calls.why: Partner relationship management means working with partners inside and outside the company to jointly bring greater value to customers.

calls.q: Overall, CRM is the process of building and maintaining profitable customer relationships by...
a: Delivering superior customer value and satisfaction
Collecting as much customer data as possible
calls.why: CRM: building and maintaining profitable relationships by delivering superior customer value and satisfaction.

wall: Share of customer: your % of their category spend

r.text: Data cage. This is where they keep the customer models.
Find a file called the Town Ledger. If Meridian has a target list, that's it.
Contact! They've got a shooter on the racks.

post.text: ...There it is. The Town Ledger. They've scored every town in Southern Ontario by customer equity. Read it. Then tell me this isn't a target list.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CAPTURING VALUE FROM CUSTOMERS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Customer lifetime value[/b] is the value of the entire stream of purchases a customer makes over a lifetime of patronage. Good CRM creates customer delight; delighted customers stay loyal and talk favourably about the company.

[b]Share of customer[/b] is the portion of the customer's purchasing that a company gets in its product categories. Firms grow it by offering greater variety, cross-selling and up-selling.

[b]Customer equity[/b] is the total combined customer lifetime values of all of the company's customers. It is a better measure of performance than current sales or market share, because sales reflect the past and customer equity suggests the future.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]BUILDING THE RIGHT RELATIONSHIPS WITH THE RIGHT CUSTOMERS[/color][/font_size]

Customers can be grouped by potential profitability and projected loyalty:

  •  [b]Strangers[/b]: low profitability, little projected loyalty. Don't invest anything in them; make money on every transaction.

  •  [b]Butterflies[/b]: profitable but not loyal. Enjoy them while you can, then cease investing when they flutter away.

  •  [b]True friends[/b]: profitable and loyal. Make continuous relationship investments to delight them and nurture, retain and grow them.

  •  [b]Barnacles[/b]: highly loyal but not very profitable. Improve their profitability, or 'fire' them if that fails.

MERIDIAN NOTE: Phase 1 towns classified 'Stranger' or 'Barnacle' are scheduled for supply withdrawal.

intel.src: A. Voss · memo to the board
intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE CHANGING MARKETING LANDSCAPE[/color][/font_size]

[b]The digital age[/b]: online, mobile and social media marketing let companies engage customers anytime and anywhere. Social media marketing joins brands to conversations; mobile marketing reaches customers on the move with real-time, location-aware offers.

[b]The growth of not-for-profit marketing[/b]: universities, hospitals, museums, charities and governments increasingly use marketing too.

[b]Rapid globalization[/b]: almost every company, large or small, is touched by global competition and global supply chains.

[b]Sustainable marketing[/b]: the call for more environmental and social responsibility. Forward-looking companies view socially responsible actions as an opportunity to do well by doing good.

Voss, margin note: 'Customers want responsibility. They will pay for the appearance of it.'

calls.q: The Town Ledger ranks towns by the total combined lifetime value of all their customers. That measure is...
calls.why: Customer equity is the total combined customer lifetime values of all the company's customers. It looks to the future, unlike current sales.

calls.q: One town is highly loyal but barely profitable. The textbook calls these customers barnacles. What strategy does it recommend?
a: Try to improve their profitability; 'fire' them only if that fails
Make money on every transaction and invest nothing
Enjoy them while they last, then stop investing
calls.why: Barnacles: improve profitability by selling them more or cutting service; fire them only as a last resort. Meridian skips straight to firing whole towns.

calls.q: Castellan's grocery app starts suggesting pharmacy products to existing shoppers. Growing the portion of a customer's spending in your categories is increasing...
calls.why: Share of customer is the portion of a customer's purchasing in your categories. Cross-selling and up-selling grow it.

calls.q: Butterflies are profitable but not loyal. The recommended strategy is to...
a: Enjoy them while you can, then stop investing when they leave
Raise their prices until they become loyal
calls.why: Butterflies: use promotional blitzes to attract them, create satisfying transactions, then cease investing once they move on.

wall: Sustainable marketing: do well by doing good

missions.loc: Kingsway Bunker · beneath Castellan's Ottawa campus

briefing.text: Ostrowski gave us a location. Kingsway: a Cold War bunker under Castellan's Ottawa campus. Their strategic planning group works down there.
Every Castellan business unit reports to Kingsway. Groceries, pharmacy, data, logistics. They plan the whole portfolio from one room.
Meridian is new, growing fast, and losing money. It can't pay for itself. Somebody else in the portfolio is feeding it.
Find the treasury servers that move that money and destroy them. Then get out before the bunker seals.
Underground, no comms, sealed doors. My favourite kind of evening.

debrief.text: They'll reroute the money, but it'll take weeks. Weeks we didn't have before.
Kessler knew our names. All of them.
Nothing leaves this team. Halifax is next. Meridian's first shipments go out through the port.

r.text: Tunnel's old. Concrete's original, cameras are new.
Comms will degrade as you go deeper. Marr will stay with you as long as she can.

post.text: Two mission statements on the planning wall. The old one and the new one. Compare them.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]STRATEGIC PLANNING[/color][/font_size]

[b]Strategic planning[/b] is the process of developing and maintaining a strategic fit between the organization's goals and capabilities and its changing marketing opportunities. It sets the stage for the rest of planning in the firm.

Companies usually prepare annual plans, long-range plans and strategic plans.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]FOUR STEPS[/color][/font_size]

  •  1. Define a market-oriented mission (corporate level).

  •  2. Set company objectives and goals (corporate level).

  •  3. Design the business portfolio (corporate level).

  •  4. Plan marketing and other functional strategies (business unit, product and market level).

Marketing plays a key role: it provides a guiding philosophy, the marketing concept, and inputs that help planners identify attractive market opportunities.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE MISSION STATEMENT[/color][/font_size]

A [b]mission statement[/b] is a statement of the organization's purpose: what it wants to accomplish in the larger environment. A clear mission statement acts as an 'invisible hand' that guides people in the organization.

Mission statements should be [b]market-oriented[/b] and defined in terms of satisfying basic customer needs. Products and technologies eventually become outdated, but basic market needs may last forever.

They should be meaningful and specific yet motivating; emphasize the company's strengths; and not be stated as making more sales or profits. Profits are only a reward for creating value for customers.

2009, market-oriented: 'We help Canadian families eat well and stay healthy, wherever they live.'

2031, product-oriented: 'Castellan sells groceries, pharmaceuticals and data services at scale.'

calls.q: 'We help Canadian families eat well and stay healthy, wherever they live.' Compared with 'We sell groceries and pharmaceuticals,' the first statement is...
a: Market-oriented: defined by the customer needs it satisfies
Product-oriented: defined by what it sells
Too specific to work as a mission
A company objective, not a mission
calls.why: Market-oriented missions define the business by the customer needs it satisfies. Products become outdated; basic needs last.

calls.q: What is the correct order of the four strategic planning steps?
a: Mission → objectives and goals → business portfolio → functional strategies
calls.why: Corporate level: define the mission, set objectives and goals, design the business portfolio. Then plan marketing and other functional strategies.

wall: SBU = a unit with its own mission

r.text: Objectives wing. CSS has a rapid-response team on this level.
Contact. Two at the end of the hall.
The mission gets turned into objectives here. Castellan sets them like a staircase: one goal supports the next.

post.text: Their objectives hierarchy is pinned up in the director's office. And next to it, the portfolio map. That's the one.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SETTING COMPANY OBJECTIVES AND GOALS[/color][/font_size]

The company's mission needs to be turned into detailed supporting objectives for each level of management. Each manager should have objectives and be responsible for reaching them.

Objectives form a hierarchy. A broad mission leads to business objectives, which lead to marketing objectives, which lead to marketing strategies and programs.

Example: build profitable customer relationships → increase market share → more effective sales force and promotion → specific marketing strategies.

Mission and objectives should be practical and measurable, so the company can track progress.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]DESIGNING THE BUSINESS PORTFOLIO[/color][/font_size]

The [b]business portfolio[/b] is the collection of businesses and products that make up the company. The best portfolio is the one that best fits the company's strengths and weaknesses to opportunities in the environment.

Business portfolio planning involves two steps: analyzing the current business portfolio and deciding which businesses should receive more, less or no investment; and shaping the future portfolio by developing strategies for growth and downsizing.

[b]Portfolio analysis[/b] is the major activity in strategic planning: management evaluates the products and businesses that make up the company.

A [b]strategic business unit (SBU)[/b] is a unit of the company that has a separate mission and objectives and that can be planned independently. It can be a division, a product line within a division, or a single product or brand.

Most standard portfolio methods evaluate SBUs on two dimensions: the attractiveness of the SBU's market or industry, and the strength of the SBU's position in that market.

calls.q: Castellan Rx has its own mission, its own objectives and can be planned independently of the grocery business. It is a...
calls.why: An SBU is a unit with a separate mission and objectives that can be planned independently: a division, product line, or single brand.

calls.q: Standard portfolio analysis evaluates SBUs on which two dimensions?
a: Attractiveness of the market and strength of the SBU's position in it
Number of employees and age of the business
calls.why: Portfolio methods look at market attractiveness and the SBU's competitive strength in that market.

Question mark: high growth, low share

r.text: This is the treasury vault. Five server stacks, one per business unit. Each screen shows market growth and relative market share.
In the BCG matrix, cash cows are the businesses that generate cash and fund everything else. Meridian is living off the cows.
Classify each stack. Plant charges on the cash cows only. Hit a star and we tip them off for nothing.

Their portfolio memo is open on the vault terminal. Grab it before we light this place up.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE BOSTON CONSULTING GROUP APPROACH[/color][/font_size]

The [b]growth-share matrix[/b] evaluates SBUs in terms of market growth rate and relative market share.

  •  [b]Stars[/b]: high-growth, high-share businesses or products. They often need heavy investment to finance rapid growth. Eventually their growth slows and they turn into cash cows.

  •  [b]Cash cows[/b]: low-growth, high-share businesses or products. These established, successful SBUs need less investment to hold their share. They produce a lot of cash that the company uses to pay its bills and support other SBUs.

  •  [b]Question marks[/b]: low-share business units in high-growth markets. They require a lot of cash to hold their share, let alone increase it. Management must decide which to build into stars and which to phase out.

  •  [b]Dogs[/b]: low-growth, low-share businesses and products. They may generate enough cash to maintain themselves but do not promise to be large sources of cash.

For each SBU, the company decides whether to [b]build, hold, harvest or divest[/b].

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PROBLEMS WITH MATRIX APPROACHES[/color][/font_size]

Matrix approaches can be difficult, time-consuming and costly to implement. They focus on classifying current businesses but provide little advice for future planning. Many companies now use more customized approaches and place responsibility for strategic planning in the hands of cross-functional teams close to their markets.

TREASURY NOTE: Grocery and Rx cash flows reallocated to MERIDIAN (question mark) until build target met.

calls.q: Meridian has a 24% market growth rate and a 0.3 relative market share. In the BCG matrix it's a...
calls.why: High growth, low share: question mark. It needs lots of cash to build share. Here it's being fed by the cash cows.

calls.q: In the classic BCG approach, what do companies do with the cash from their cash cows?
a: Invest it to support stars and question marks
Pay it all out as dividends
calls.why: Funds from mature, successful cash cows support promising stars and question marks, hoping to turn them into future cash cows.

calls.q: A major problem with matrix approaches like BCG is that they...

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PARTNERING WITH OTHER COMPANY DEPARTMENTS[/color][/font_size]

Success depends not only on how well each department performs its work but also on how well the activities of the various departments are coordinated. Departments tend to maximize their own interests; marketers must get all departments to think like the customer.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PARTNERING WITH OTHERS IN THE MARKETING SYSTEM[/color][/font_size]

The [b]value delivery network[/b] is made up of the company, suppliers, distributors and, ultimately, customers who partner with each other to improve the performance of the entire system.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING STRATEGY AND THE MARKETING MIX[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing strategy[/b] is the marketing logic by which the company hopes to create customer value and achieve profitable customer relationships. The company decides which customers it will serve (segmentation and targeting) and how (differentiation and positioning).

[b]Market segmentation[/b]: dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers who have different needs, characteristics or behaviours, and who might require separate marketing strategies or mixes. A [b]market segment[/b] is a group of consumers who respond in a similar way to a given set of marketing efforts.

[b]Market targeting[/b]: evaluating each market segment's attractiveness and selecting one or more segments to serve.

[b]Positioning[/b]: arranging for a market offering to occupy a clear, distinctive and desirable place relative to competing products in the minds of target consumers. [b]Differentiation[/b]: actually differentiating the market offering to create superior customer value.

The [b]marketing mix[/b] is the set of tactical marketing tools (product, price, place and promotion) that the firm blends to produce the response it wants in the target market.

  •  [b]Product[/b]: the goods-and-services combination the company offers.

  •  [b]Price[/b]: the amount customers must pay to obtain the product.

  •  [b]Place[/b]: company activities that make the product available to target consumers.

  •  [b]Promotion[/b]: activities that communicate the merits of the product and persuade target customers to buy it. Its tools include [b]advertising[/b], [b]personal selling[/b], [b]sales promotion[/b] (short-term incentives to encourage the purchase or sale of a product or service), public relations and direct and digital marketing.

The four Ps take the seller's view. From the buyer's view they might be the [b]four As[/b]: acceptability (product), affordability (price), accessibility (place) and awareness (promotion).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]ANALYSIS: SWOT[/color][/font_size]

A [b]SWOT analysis[/b] is an overall evaluation of the company's strengths (S), weaknesses (W), opportunities (O) and threats (T). Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. The goal is to match the company's strengths to attractive opportunities in the environment, while eliminating or overcoming the weaknesses and minimizing the threats.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PLANNING[/color][/font_size]

A marketing plan typically includes an executive summary; current marketing situation; threats and opportunities analysis; objectives and issues; marketing strategy; action programs; budgets; and controls.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]IMPLEMENTATION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing implementation[/b] is turning marketing strategies and plans into marketing actions to accomplish strategic marketing objectives. Planning addresses what and why; implementation addresses who, where, when and how.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]ORGANIZATION[/color][/font_size]

Common forms: a [b]functional organization[/b] (activities headed by functional specialists), a [b]geographic organization[/b] (people assigned to countries, regions and districts), [b]product management[/b] (managers for products or brands), [b]market or customer management[/b] (managers for markets or customers), or a combination.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING CONTROL[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing control[/b] is measuring and evaluating the results of marketing strategies and plans, and taking corrective action to ensure that the objectives are achieved.

Operating control checks ongoing performance against the annual plan. Strategic control looks at whether the company's basic strategies are well matched to its opportunities.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING RETURN ON INVESTMENT[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing return on investment (marketing ROI)[/b] is the net return from a marketing investment divided by the costs of the marketing investment. It measures the profits generated by investments in marketing activities.

Companies can assess marketing ROI with standard marketing performance measures (brand awareness, sales, market share) and customer-centred measures (customer acquisition, retention, lifetime value, customer equity). Many assemble these into [b]marketing dashboards[/b] to monitor strategic marketing performance.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING INFORMATION AND CUSTOMER INSIGHTS[/color][/font_size]

To create value for customers, companies must first gain fresh, deep insights into what customers need and want.

[b]Customer insights[/b] are fresh marketing-information-based understandings of customers and the marketplace that become the basis for creating customer value, engagement and relationships.

[b]Big data[/b] refers to the huge and complex data sets generated by today's sophisticated information generation, collection, storage and analysis technologies. Most marketing managers are overloaded with data. The challenge is to turn it into insight.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE MARKETING INFORMATION SYSTEM[/color][/font_size]

A [b]marketing information system (MIS)[/b] consists of people and procedures dedicated to assessing information needs, developing the needed information, and helping decision makers use the information to generate and validate actionable customer and market insights.

A good MIS balances the information users would like to have against what they really need and what is feasible to offer. Information costs money; the value it adds must exceed its cost.

[b]Internal databases[/b] are collections of consumer and market information obtained from data sources within the company network.

Sources include company employees, competitors' annual reports and public filings, trade shows, websites and social media, and buying and analyzing competitors' products.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING RESEARCH[/color][/font_size]

[b]Marketing research[/b] is the systematic design, collection, analysis and reporting of data relevant to a specific marketing situation facing an organization.

The marketing research process has four steps: defining the problem and research objectives; developing the research plan for collecting information; implementing the research plan (collecting and analyzing the data); and interpreting and reporting the findings.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]DEFINING THE PROBLEM AND RESEARCH OBJECTIVES[/color][/font_size]

Defining the problem and research objectives is often the hardest step. A project might have one of three types of objectives:

  •  [b]Exploratory research[/b]: to gather preliminary information that will help define problems and suggest hypotheses.

  •  [b]Descriptive research[/b]: to describe things, such as the market potential for a product or the demographics and attitudes of consumers who buy it.

  •  [b]Causal research[/b]: to test hypotheses about cause-and-effect relationships.

Managers often start with exploratory research and later follow with descriptive or causal research.

  •  [b]Survey research[/b]: gathering primary data by asking people questions about their knowledge, attitudes, preferences and buying behaviour. Best suited to descriptive information. It is flexible, but people may be unable or unwilling to answer accurately.

  •  [b]Experimental research[/b]: gathering primary data by selecting matched groups of subjects, giving them different treatments, controlling related factors, and checking for differences in group responses. Best suited to causal information.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CONTACT METHODS[/color][/font_size]

Information can be collected by [b]mail, telephone, personal interview, or online[/b].

[b]Personal interviewing[/b] takes two forms: individual and group. [b]Focus group interviewing[/b] brings six to ten people together with a trained moderator to talk about a product, service or organization. It is one of the major qualitative tools, but small samples make it hard to generalize, and moderators must avoid bias.

[b]Online marketing research[/b] collects primary data through internet and mobile surveys, online focus groups, consumer tracking, experiments, and online panels and brand communities. [b]Online focus groups[/b] gather a small group of people online with a trained moderator.

[b]Behavioural targeting[/b] uses online consumer tracking data and analytics to target advertisements and marketing offers to specific consumers.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SAMPLING PLAN[/color][/font_size]

A [b]sample[/b] is a segment of the population selected for marketing research to represent the population as a whole. Designing it takes three decisions: [b]who[/b] is to be studied (the sampling unit), [b]how many[/b] (sample size), and [b]how they are chosen[/b] (sampling procedure).

  •  Probability samples: [b]simple random[/b] (every member has a known and equal chance), [b]stratified random[/b] (population divided into mutually exclusive groups such as age, random samples from each), [b]cluster or area[/b] (population divided into groups such as blocks; a sample of groups is interviewed).

  •  Nonprobability samples: [b]convenience[/b] (easiest to reach), [b]judgment[/b] (researcher picks good prospects for accurate information), [b]quota[/b] (a prescribed number from each of several categories).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]RESEARCH INSTRUMENTS[/color][/font_size]

Two main instruments: the [b]questionnaire[/b] (most common; administered in person, by phone or online; closed-end or open-end questions) and [b]mechanical instruments[/b] (people meters, checkout scanners, eye cameras, brain-activity monitors).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]IMPLEMENTING, INTERPRETING AND REPORTING[/color][/font_size]

Implementing the plan means collecting, processing and analyzing the information. The data collection phase is generally the most expensive and the most subject to error.

The researcher must then [b]interpret the findings, draw conclusions and report them[/b] to management, presenting important findings and insights useful for major decisions. Interpretation should not be left only to researchers: managers know the problem and the decisions that must be made.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]ANALYZING AND USING MARKETING INFORMATION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Customer relationship management (CRM)[/b] here means managing detailed information about individual customers and carefully managing customer [b]touch points[/b] in order to maximize customer loyalty. A touch point is every contact between a customer and the company: purchases, sales contacts, service calls, website and social media visits, surveys.

[b]Marketing analytics[/b] consists of the analysis tools, technologies and processes by which marketers dig out meaningful patterns in big data to gain customer insights and gauge marketing performance.

[b]Artificial intelligence (AI)[/b] is technology by which machines think and learn in a way that looks and feels human, but with much more analytical capacity.

Marketing information has no value until it is used to make better decisions; it must be distributed to the right people at the right time.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]OTHER MARKETING INFORMATION CONSIDERATIONS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Small businesses and not-for-profits[/b] can obtain good marketing insights through observation and informal surveys at low cost, using secondary data from government and associations.

[b]International marketing research[/b] follows the same steps but faces extra problems: finding good secondary data, the cost of collecting primary data, language and cultural differences, and different response patterns.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PUBLIC POLICY AND ETHICS[/color][/font_size]

Two major concerns: [b]intrusions on consumer privacy[/b] (consumers may resent research and data collection they see as intrusive, or worry about how their information is used), and the [b]misuse of research findings[/b] (research studies can be used as powerful persuasion tools, designed or interpreted to support a sponsor's preferred conclusion).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MODEL OF BUYER BEHAVIOUR[/color][/font_size]

[b]Consumer buyer behaviour[/b] refers to the buying behaviour of final consumers: individuals and households that buy goods and services for personal consumption. All of them combined make up the [b]consumer market[/b].

Marketing stimuli (the four Ps) and other stimuli (economic, technological, social, cultural) enter the consumer's [b]black box[/b] and produce responses: buying attitudes and preferences, purchase behaviour (what, when, where, how much), and brand and company relationship behaviour.

A [b]subculture[/b] is a group of people with shared value systems based on common life experiences and situations. Important Canadian subcultures include regional (East coast, West coast, Northern), francophone, Indigenous, ethnic (such as Chinese and South Asian Canadians) and mature consumers.

A [b]total market strategy[/b] integrates ethnic themes and cross-cultural perspectives within a brand's mainstream marketing, appealing to consumer similarities across subcultural segments rather than differences.

[b]Social class[/b] refers to relatively permanent and ordered divisions in a society whose members share similar values, interests and behaviours. It is measured by a combination of occupation, income, education, wealth and other variables.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MOTIVATION[/color][/font_size]

A [b]motive (or drive)[/b] is a need that is sufficiently pressing to direct the person to seek satisfaction of the need.

[b]Freud[/b] assumed that people are largely unconscious about the real psychological forces shaping their behaviour; buying decisions are affected by subconscious motives. [b]Motivation research[/b] uses in-depth, qualitative research to probe consumers' hidden, subconscious motivations.

[b]Maslow[/b] arranged human needs in a hierarchy, from most pressing at the bottom to least pressing at the top: [b]physiological[/b] needs (hunger, thirst), [b]safety[/b] needs (security, protection), [b]social[/b] needs (belonging, love), [b]esteem[/b] needs (self-esteem, recognition, status) and [b]self-actualization[/b] needs (self-development and realization). A person tries to satisfy the most important need first.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PERCEPTION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Perception[/b] is the process by which people select, organize and interpret information to form a meaningful picture of the world. People form different perceptions of the same stimulus because of three perceptual processes:

  •  [b]Selective attention[/b]: the tendency for people to screen out most of the information to which they are exposed.

  •  [b]Selective distortion[/b]: the tendency to interpret information in a way that will support what people already believe.

  •  [b]Selective retention[/b]: people forget much of what they learn but tend to retain information that supports their attitudes and beliefs.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]LEARNING, BELIEFS AND ATTITUDES[/color][/font_size]

[b]Learning[/b] describes changes in an individual's behaviour arising from experience. It occurs through the interplay of [b]drives, stimuli, cues, responses and reinforcement[/b].

A [b]belief[/b] is a descriptive thought that a person holds about something. An [b]attitude[/b] is a person's consistently favourable or unfavourable evaluations, feelings and tendencies toward an object or idea. Attitudes are difficult to change.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE BUYER DECISION PROCESS[/color][/font_size]

  •  [b]Need recognition[/b]: the buyer recognizes a problem or need, triggered by internal or external stimuli.

  •  [b]Information search[/b]: sources include [b]personal[/b] (family, friends, neighbours), [b]commercial[/b] (advertising, salespeople, websites, packaging, displays), [b]public[/b] (mass media, rating organizations, social media, online reviews) and [b]experiential[/b] (handling, examining, using the product).

  •  [b]Evaluation of alternatives[/b]: how the consumer processes information to choose among brands.

  •  [b]Purchase decision[/b]: generally the most preferred brand, but two factors can come between purchase intention and decision: [b]the attitudes of others[/b] and [b]unexpected situational factors[/b].

  •  [b]Postpurchase behaviour[/b]: the relationship between the consumer's expectations and the product's perceived performance. [b]Cognitive dissonance[/b] is buyer discomfort caused by postpurchase conflict.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]NEW PRODUCTS[/color][/font_size]

A [b]new product[/b] is a good, service or idea perceived by some potential customers as new. The [b]adoption process[/b] is the mental process through which an individual passes from first hearing about an innovation to final adoption: [b]awareness, interest, evaluation, trial, adoption[/b].

Individual differences in innovativeness: [b]innovators[/b] (2.5%), [b]early adopters[/b] (13.5%), [b]early mainstream[/b] (34%), [b]late mainstream[/b] (34%) and [b]lagging adopters[/b] (16%).

Five product characteristics affect the rate of adoption: [b]relative advantage[/b] (appears superior to existing products), [b]compatibility[/b] (fits values and experiences), [b]complexity[/b] (difficult to understand or use), [b]divisibility[/b] (can be tried on a limited basis) and [b]communicability[/b] (results can be observed or described to others).

calls.q: Castellan offers a free one-week trial of its new subscription before customers commit. Which product characteristic speeds adoption here?

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]BUSINESS MARKETS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Business buyer behaviour[/b] is the buying behaviour of organizations that buy goods and services for use in the production of other products and services, or to resell or rent them at a profit.

Compared with consumer markets, business markets have [b]fewer but larger buyers[/b]; demand is [b]derived demand[/b] (business demand that ultimately comes from the demand for consumer goods); buying involves [b]more decision participants and more professional purchasing effort[/b]; decisions are more complex and the process more formalized; and buyer and seller work closely together and build long-term relationships.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MAJOR TYPES OF BUYING SITUATIONS[/color][/font_size]

  •  [b]Straight rebuy[/b]: the buyer routinely reorders something without modifications.

  •  [b]Modified rebuy[/b]: the buyer wants to modify product specifications, prices, terms or suppliers.

  •  [b]New task[/b]: the buyer purchases a product or service for the first time.

[b]Systems selling (solutions selling)[/b] is buying a packaged solution to a problem from a single seller, avoiding all the separate decisions involved in a complex buying situation.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PARTICIPANTS AND INFLUENCES[/color][/font_size]

The [b]buying centre[/b] is all the individuals and units that play a role in the purchase decision-making process: the actual [b]users[/b], those who [b]influence[/b] the decision, those who do the actual [b]buying[/b], those who make the [b]decision[/b], and [b]gatekeepers[/b] who control buying information.

Business buyers are subject to [b]environmental, organizational, interpersonal and individual[/b] influences. They respond to both economic and personal factors.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]THE BUSINESS BUYER DECISION PROCESS[/color][/font_size]

The [b]business buying process[/b] is the decision process by which business buyers determine which products and services their organizations need to purchase, then find, evaluate and choose among alternative suppliers and brands.

Eight stages, all of them in a new task situation: [b]problem recognition, general need description, product specification, supplier search, proposal solicitation, supplier selection, order-routine specification, and performance review[/b]. Modified and straight rebuys may skip stages.

[b]Supplier development[/b] is the systematic development of networks of supplier-partners to ensure an appropriate and dependable supply of products and materials.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]ENGAGING BUSINESS BUYERS DIGITALLY[/color][/font_size]

[b]E-procurement[/b] is purchasing through electronic connections between buyers and sellers, usually online. It gives buyers access to new suppliers, lowers purchasing costs, and hastens order processing and delivery.

B-to-B marketers also use digital and social media marketing (websites, blogs, mobile apps, online video, social networks) to engage business customers and manage relationships anytime, anywhere.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]DESIGNING A CUSTOMER-DRIVEN STRATEGY[/color][/font_size]

Four steps. [b]Segmentation[/b]: dividing a market into smaller segments of buyers with distinct needs, characteristics or behaviours that might require separate strategies or mixes. [b]Targeting[/b]: evaluating each segment's attractiveness and selecting one or more to enter. [b]Differentiation[/b]: differentiating the market offering to create superior customer value. [b]Positioning[/b]: arranging for an offering to occupy a clear, distinctive and desirable place relative to competing products in the minds of target consumers.

The first two decide [b]which customers to serve[/b]; the last two decide [b]the value proposition[/b]: how to create value for them.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SEGMENTING CONSUMER MARKETS[/color][/font_size]

There is no single way to segment a market. Major variables are geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural.

[b]Geographic segmentation[/b] divides the market into different geographical units such as nations, regions, provinces, cities or even neighbourhoods. Many companies localize products, advertising and promotion to fit the needs of individual regions, cities and neighbourhoods.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]DEMOGRAPHIC SEGMENTATION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Demographic segmentation[/b] divides the market into segments based on variables such as age, life-cycle stage, gender, income, occupation, education, religion, ethnicity and generation. Demographic factors are the most popular bases for segmenting customer groups, partly because they're easier to measure.

  •  [b]Age and life-cycle segmentation[/b]: offering different products or using different marketing approaches for different age and life-cycle groups.

  •  [b]Gender segmentation[/b]: different products and marketing approaches for men and women.

  •  [b]Income segmentation[/b]: different products or marketing programs for affluent, middle-income and low-income consumers.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PSYCHOGRAPHIC SEGMENTATION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Psychographic segmentation[/b] divides buyers into segments based on lifestyle or personality characteristics. People in the same demographic group can have very different psychographic characteristics.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]BEHAVIOURAL SEGMENTATION[/color][/font_size]

[b]Behavioural segmentation[/b] divides buyers based on their knowledge, attitudes, uses or responses to a product. Many marketers believe it is the best starting point.

  •  [b]Occasion segmentation[/b]: according to occasions when buyers get the idea to buy, make the purchase or use it.

  •  [b]Benefit segmentation[/b]: according to the different benefits consumers seek from the product.

  •  [b]User status[/b]: non-users, ex-users, potential users, first-time users and regular users.

  •  [b]Usage rate[/b]: light, medium and heavy users.

  •  [b]Loyalty status[/b]: completely loyal, somewhat loyal, or no loyalty to a brand.

Using multiple bases: marketers rarely limit themselves to one or a few variables; they combine several to identify smaller, better-defined target groups.

calls.q: Two 40-year-old accountants with the same income: one hikes every weekend, one is a homebody gamer. Which variable separates them?
calls.why: People in the same demographic group can have very different psychographic profiles.

calls.q: Selling extra hot soup in the winter months and more cold drinks in summer is...
calls.why: Occasion segmentation groups buyers by when they get the idea to buy, purchase or use the product.

calls.q: Many marketers believe the best starting point for building segments is...
calls.why: Behavioural segmentation (knowledge, attitudes, uses, responses) is often the best starting point.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SEGMENTING BUSINESS MARKETS[/color][/font_size]

Consumer and business marketers use many of the same variables. Business marketers also use customer [b]operating characteristics[/b], [b]purchasing approaches[/b], [b]situational factors[/b] and [b]personal characteristics[/b]. Many companies set up separate systems for dealing with larger or multiple-location customers.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SEGMENTING INTERNATIONAL MARKETS[/color][/font_size]

Companies can segment international markets by [b]geographic location[/b], [b]economic factors[/b], [b]political and legal factors[/b], and [b]cultural factors[/b].

[b]Intermarket (cross-market) segmentation[/b] forms segments of consumers who have similar needs and buying behaviours even though they are located in different countries.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]REQUIREMENTS FOR EFFECTIVE SEGMENTATION[/color][/font_size]

To be useful, market segments must be:

  •  [b]Measurable[/b]: size, purchasing power and profiles can be measured.

  •  [b]Accessible[/b]: the segments can be effectively reached and served.

  •  [b]Substantial[/b]: large or profitable enough to serve.

  •  [b]Differentiable[/b]: conceptually distinguishable and respond differently to different marketing mix elements.

  •  [b]Actionable[/b]: effective programs can be designed for attracting and serving them.

calls.q: Teenagers in Toronto, Tokyo and São Paulo share similar music and phone habits, so a brand targets them as one global segment. That's...

calls.q: Castellan identifies a segment it can measure and that is big enough, but it has no way to reach those customers. Which requirement fails?
calls.why: Accessible means the segments can be effectively reached and served.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]EVALUATING MARKET SEGMENTS[/color][/font_size]

A firm looks at three factors: [b]segment size and growth[/b]; [b]segment structural attractiveness[/b] (competitors, substitute products, the relative power of buyers and of suppliers); and [b]company objectives and resources[/b].

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SELECTING TARGET MARKET SEGMENTS[/color][/font_size]

A [b]target market[/b] is a set of buyers who share common needs or characteristics that a company decides to serve. Strategies run from very broad to very narrow:

  •  [b]Undifferentiated (mass) marketing[/b]: ignore segment differences and go after the whole market with one offer.

  •  [b]Differentiated (segmented) marketing[/b]: target several segments and design separate offers for each.

  •  [b]Concentrated (niche) marketing[/b]: go after a large share of one or a few smaller segments or niches.

  •  [b]Micromarketing[/b]: tailor products and programs to the tastes of specific individuals and local customer segments. It includes [b]local marketing[/b] (tailoring to cities, neighbourhoods, even specific stores) and [b]individual marketing[/b] (tailoring to the needs and preferences of individual customers; also called one-to-one marketing, mass customization and markets-of-one).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SOCIALLY RESPONSIBLE TARGET MARKETING[/color][/font_size]

Target marketing sometimes generates controversy. The biggest issues usually involve targeting vulnerable or disadvantaged consumers with controversial or potentially harmful products. The issue is not who is targeted, but how and for what. Socially responsible marketing calls for segmentation and targeting that serve not just the company's interests, but also the interests of those targeted.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PRODUCT POSITION[/color][/font_size]

A [b]product position[/b] is the way a product is defined by consumers on important attributes: the place it occupies in consumers' minds relative to competing products. Consumers position products with or without the help of marketers.

[b]Perceptual positioning maps[/b] show consumer perceptions of a brand versus competing products on important buying dimensions.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CHOOSING A DIFFERENTIATION AND POSITIONING STRATEGY[/color][/font_size]

Three steps: identify a set of differentiating competitive advantages; choose the right competitive advantages; select an overall positioning strategy.

A [b]competitive advantage[/b] is an advantage over competitors gained by offering greater customer value, either by having lower prices or providing more benefits that justify higher prices.

Firms can differentiate along the lines of [b]product[/b] (features, performance, style and design), [b]services[/b] (speedy, convenient or careful delivery), [b]channels[/b] (coverage, expertise, performance), [b]people[/b] (hiring and training better people) or [b]image[/b] (brand image conveying distinctive benefits and positioning).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CHOOSING THE RIGHT COMPETITIVE ADVANTAGES[/color][/font_size]

A difference is worth establishing if it is [b]important[/b] (delivers a highly valued benefit), [b]distinctive[/b] (competitors don't offer it, or it's offered more distinctively), [b]superior[/b] (better than other ways to get the benefit), [b]communicable[/b] (visible to buyers), [b]pre-emptive[/b] (competitors can't easily copy it), [b]affordable[/b] (buyers can pay for it) and [b]profitable[/b] (the company can introduce it profitably).

Some marketers recommend a [b]unique selling proposition (USP)[/b]: pick one attribute and tout yourself as 'number one' on it. Others think companies should position on more than one differentiator.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]SELECTING AN OVERALL POSITIONING STRATEGY[/color][/font_size]

A [b]value proposition[/b] is the full positioning of a brand: the full mix of benefits on which it is positioned. Five winning value propositions:

  •  [b]More for more[/b]: the most upscale product or service at a higher price to cover the higher costs.

  •  [b]More for the same[/b]: attacking a competitor's more-for-more positioning by introducing a brand that offers comparable quality at a lower price.

  •  [b]The same for less[/b]: a powerful value proposition; everyone likes a good deal.

  •  [b]Less for much less[/b]: offering products that meet consumers' lower performance or quality requirements at a much lower price.

  •  [b]More for less[/b]: the winning proposition in theory, but difficult to sustain in the long run.

Losing propositions, such as less for more or the same for more, invite competitors to steal the brand's customers.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]DEVELOPING A POSITIONING STATEMENT[/color][/font_size]

A company's positioning should be summed up in a [b]positioning statement[/b], which follows the form: [b]To (target segment and need), our (brand) is (concept) that (point of difference).[/b]

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]COMMUNICATING AND DELIVERING THE CHOSEN POSITION[/color][/font_size]

Once a position is chosen, the company must take strong steps to deliver and communicate it to target consumers. All of the marketing mix efforts must support the positioning strategy. Positions should evolve with changing needs and competitors.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PRODUCTS, SERVICES AND EXPERIENCES[/color][/font_size]

A [b]product[/b] is anything that can be offered to a market for attention, acquisition, use or consumption that might satisfy a want or need. Products include physical objects, services, events, persons, places, organizations, ideas, or mixes of these.

A [b]service[/b] is an activity, benefit or satisfaction offered for sale that is essentially intangible and does not result in the ownership of anything.

A company's market offering often includes both tangible goods and services, ranging from pure tangible goods to pure services. Many firms now create and manage [b]customer experiences[/b] with their products or company.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]LEVELS OF PRODUCT AND SERVICES[/color][/font_size]

  •  [b]Augmented product[/b]: additional consumer services and benefits built around the core and actual products, such as warranties, delivery, after-sale service and support.

Consumers see products as complex bundles of benefits that satisfy their needs.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]CONSUMER PRODUCTS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Consumer products[/b] are products and services bought by final consumers for personal consumption. Classified by how consumers buy them:

  •  [b]Convenience products[/b]: bought frequently, immediately, with minimal comparison and buying effort. Low price, widespread distribution. (Laundry detergent, candy, fast food.)

  •  [b]Shopping products[/b]: less frequently purchased; customers carefully compare suitability, quality, price and style. Selective distribution, fewer outlets. (Furniture, clothing, major appliances.)

  •  [b]Specialty products[/b]: unique characteristics or brand identification for which a significant group of buyers is willing to make a special purchase effort. (Luxury cars, high-end watches, specialized medical services.)

  •  [b]Unsought products[/b]: products the consumer either does not know about or knows about but does not normally think of buying. (Life insurance, preplanned funeral services, blood donations.) They require a lot of advertising and personal selling.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]INDUSTRIAL PRODUCTS[/color][/font_size]

[b]Industrial products[/b] are bought by individuals and organizations for further processing or for use in conducting a business. Three groups: [b]materials and parts[/b] (raw materials and manufactured materials and parts), [b]capital items[/b] (installations and accessory equipment) and [b]supplies and services[/b] (operating supplies, maintenance and repair items, business advisory services).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]ORGANIZATIONS, PERSONS, PLACES AND IDEAS[/color][/font_size]

Marketers also market organizations (corporate image marketing), persons, places and ideas. [b]Social marketing[/b] is the use of traditional business marketing concepts and tools to encourage behaviours that will create individual and societal well-being.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]INDIVIDUAL PRODUCT AND SERVICE DECISIONS[/color][/font_size]

Five decisions: [b]product attributes, branding, packaging, labelling and logos, and product support services[/b].

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PRODUCT ATTRIBUTES[/color][/font_size]

[b]Product quality[/b] is the characteristics of a product or service that bear on its ability to satisfy stated or implied customer needs. It has two dimensions: [b]quality level[/b] (performance quality: the product's ability to perform its functions) and [b]quality consistency[/b] (conformance quality: freedom from defects and consistency in delivering a targeted level of performance).

[b]Features[/b] are a competitive tool for differentiating the company's product from competitors' products. [b]Style[/b] describes the appearance of a product; [b]design[/b] goes to the very heart of a product, contributing to usefulness as well as looks.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PACKAGING, LABELLING AND SUPPORT[/color][/font_size]

[b]Packaging[/b] involves designing and producing the container or wrapper for a product. Its primary function is to hold and protect, but it has become an important marketing tool too.

[b]Labels and logos[/b] identify the product or brand, describe several things about the product, and help promote the brand. In Canada, labelling is regulated by acts such as the [b]Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act[/b], which governs what must appear on labels (such as bilingual product information) and prohibits misleading labelling.

[b]Product support services[/b] augment actual products. Companies should design support services to meet target customers' needs profitably.

calls.q: Assure promises every delivery will arrive complete and on time, every week, with no defects. That's which dimension of quality?
calls.why: Quality consistency is freedom from defects and consistency in delivering a targeted level of performance.

calls.q: Which Canadian act governs what must appear on product labels and prohibits misleading labelling?
calls.why: The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act regulates label content and prohibits misleading labelling.

calls.q: Which list contains the five individual product and service decisions?

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PRODUCT LINE DECISIONS[/color][/font_size]

A [b]product line[/b] is a group of products that are closely related because they function in a similar manner, are sold to the same customer groups, are marketed through the same types of outlets, or fall within given price ranges.

The major line decision involves [b]product line length[/b]: the number of items in the line. A line is too short if adding items increases profits, too long if dropping items increases profits.

A company can lengthen its line by [b]product line filling[/b] (adding more items within the present range of the line: for extra profits, to satisfy dealers, to use excess capacity, to be the leading full-line company, or to plug holes against competitors) or by [b]product line stretching[/b] (lengthening the line beyond its current range: [b]downward[/b], [b]upward[/b], or [b]both ways[/b]).

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]PRODUCT MIX DECISIONS[/color][/font_size]

The [b]product mix (or product portfolio)[/b] consists of all the product lines and items that a particular seller offers for sale. It has four important dimensions:

  •  [b]Width[/b]: the number of different product lines the company carries.

  •  [b]Length[/b]: the total number of items the company carries within its product lines.

  •  [b]Depth[/b]: the number of versions offered of each product in the line.

  •  [b]Consistency[/b]: how closely related the various product lines are in end use, production requirements, distribution channels or other ways.

calls.q: Castellan adds 'Assure Basic', a cheaper tier below its existing range, to reach lower-income households. That's...

calls.q: Castellan carries groceries, pharmacy, home goods and data services: four different product lines. That number is the product mix...
calls.why: Width is the number of product lines. Length is total items; depth is versions per product; consistency is how related the lines are.

calls.q: Castellan sells its store-brand pain reliever in 12 sizes and formulas. That's product mix...
calls.why: Depth refers to the number of versions offered of each product in the line.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]FOUR SERVICE CHARACTERISTICS[/color][/font_size]

  •  [b]Service intangibility[/b]: services cannot be seen, tasted, felt, heard or smelled before they are bought. Buyers look for signals of quality.

  •  [b]Service inseparability[/b]: services are produced and consumed at the same time and cannot be separated from their providers, whether people or machines.

  •  [b]Service variability[/b]: the quality of services depends on who provides them as well as when, where and how they are provided.

  •  [b]Service perishability[/b]: services cannot be stored for later sale or use.

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MARKETING STRATEGIES FOR SERVICE FIRMS[/color][/font_size]

The [b]service profit chain[/b] links service firm profits with employee and customer satisfaction: internal service quality → satisfied and productive service employees → greater service value → satisfied and loyal customers → healthy service profits and growth.

Service marketing requires more than the four Ps. [b]Internal marketing[/b] means orienting and motivating customer-contact employees and supporting service people to work as a team to provide customer satisfaction. [b]Interactive marketing[/b] means service quality depends heavily on the quality of the buyer-seller interaction during the service encounter.

Service firms must manage [b]service differentiation[/b] (offer, delivery, image), [b]service quality[/b] (consistently meeting or exceeding expectations; good service recovery can turn angry customers into loyal ones), and [b]service productivity[/b] (training, more efficient processes, technology), without taking quality out of the service.

calls.why: Service perishability means services cannot be stored for later sale or use.

calls.q: Assure's support quality depends on which agent answers, and when. That's service...

calls.q: The service profit chain says healthy profits ultimately start with...

calls.why: Internal service quality → satisfied employees → greater service value → satisfied, loyal customers → healthy profits and growth.

calls.q: Training and motivating customer-contact staff to work as a team for customer satisfaction is...
calls.why: Internal marketing orients and motivates employees; interactive marketing is the quality of the buyer-seller interaction.

intel.bb:
[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]BRAND EQUITY AND BRAND VALUE[/color][/font_size]

A [b]brand[/b] is a name, term, sign, symbol or design, or a combination of these, that identifies the products or services of one seller and differentiates them from competitors'.

[b]Brand equity[/b] is the differential effect that knowing the brand name has on customer response to the product or its marketing. [b]Brand value[/b] is the total financial value of a brand.

Young & Rubicam's [b]BrandAsset Valuator[/b] measures brand strength on four dimensions: [b]differentiation[/b], [b]relevance[/b], [b]knowledge[/b] and [b]esteem[/b].

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]BUILDING STRONG BRANDS[/color][/font_size]

  •  [b]Brand positioning[/b]: at three levels: product [b]attributes[/b] (the lowest level), desirable [b]benefits[/b], and strong [b]beliefs and values[/b] (the strongest).

  •  [b]Brand name selection[/b]: suggests benefits and qualities; easy to say, recognize and remember; distinctive; extendable; translatable; capable of registration and legal protection.

  •  [b]Brand sponsorship[/b]: a [b]manufacturer's (national) brand[/b]; a [b]store (private) brand[/b] created and owned by a reseller; [b]licensing[/b] (using names or symbols created by other companies for a fee); or [b]co-branding[/b] (using the established brand names of two different companies on the same product).

  •  [b]Brand development[/b]: [b]line extensions[/b] (existing brand name, new forms, colours, sizes, ingredients or flavours of an existing category), [b]brand extensions[/b] (extending a current brand name to new or modified products in a new category), [b]multibrands[/b] (additional brands in the same category) and [b]new brands[/b].

[font_size=22][color=#f0c060]MANAGING BRANDS[/color][/font_size]

Companies must manage their brands carefully: communicate the positioning continuously, engage customers with the brand at every touch point, and periodically audit their brands' strengths and weaknesses.

boards.title: WHO IS MERIDIAN FOR?
boards.lead: Ostrowski talked for six hours. Somebody inside Castellan is funding Meridian, and Voss knows Major Hale's name.
